name: ¿Por Qué No? Taqueria
why: The colorful, crowded room and handmade-tortilla tacos carry atmosphere and signature. It is a very good version of a common thing, pricier than most taquerias, with a second shop on Hawthorne and about as far from under the radar as Portland gets, so uniqueness sits mid-pack.
story: ¿Por Qué No? opened on Mississippi in 2004, and owner Bryan Steelman built its loud, colorful room as a tribute to the hole-in-the-wall spots he visited in Mexico. Tortillas are handmade. Lines are common on Taco Tuesdays and sunny days, and in 2026 Willamette Week readers voted it the city's best taco and best Mexican.
tagline: Readers' top taco, on Mississippi since 2004
order: A few tacos, including the pollo verde, chicken slow-cooked in tomatillo salsa. Go off-peak: the line builds on Taco Tuesdays and nice days.
practical: Expect a line on Taco Tuesdays and sunny days
Covered patio at the Mississippi shop
Second shop at 4635 SE Hawthorne Blvd
flags: Location count: two (3524 N Mississippi Ave and 4635 SE Hawthorne Blvd) per Wikipedia, which was edited in 2026. Searches found no third shop. Under our 4-location chain line.

Very well known: 2026 Willamette Week readers' poll winner for Best Mexican, Best Taco and Best Family-Friendly (also won in 2022 and 2024), Oregonian readers' best taqueria in 2014, covered by WW, the Oregonian, Portland Mercury, Portland Monthly and Travel Portland. Reviewer may judge it too famous for the guide.
Hours unconfirmed: only directory hours turned up. The when field (midday, evening) is a guess.
Most facts come from Wikipedia, which cites WW, USA Today and Frommer's pieces from 2005 to 2014. Handmade tortillas, the lines and the pollo verde may be dated.
Discovery's carnitas taco pick could not be sourced; replaced with pollo verde (WW 2005 via Wikipedia).
Newest dated evidence it is open: WW readers' poll, Jul 22, 2026 (read from a copy of the page saved earlier this run); Wikipedia also notes Dumpling Week 2026.
Address 3524 N Mississippi Ave matches Wikipedia; one listing says 3525.

name: Queen of Sheba
why: Three decades as one of the places that taught Portland Ethiopian food carries the story mark. The city has several good Ethiopian kitchens now, and I found little on the room beyond casual and lively, so uniqueness and atmosphere sit in the middle.
story: Queen of Sheba opened in the 1990s and gave a lot of Portlanders their first taste of Ethiopian food. The Black-owned restaurant on MLK also got injera, berbere and other Ethiopian imports into markets around town. Willamette Week readers keep voting it the city's best Ethiopian, most recently in 2026.
order: Spice runs medium-hot across the board. Heat-seekers should get the tibbsi kinttishara, mushrooms sauteed in berbere; for something gentler, order an alicha.
practical: Dishes come medium-hot unless you order a mild alicha
flags: Hours unconfirmed. Listings disagree: older guides show 5-10 pm daily plus Thu-Sat lunch, newer listings show closed Mon-Tue and 5-9 pm, and a review says it was closed during posted hours. The when field (evening) rests on every listing showing dinner from 5 pm. Worth a call.

Dish picks, the medium-hot spice note and the imports detail come from a 2018 Eater Portland piece as quoted on Wikipedia; the Eater original was not opened. Whether it still supplies markets is unknown.
Opened in the 1990s per Wikipedia (citing KOIN and the Portland Mercury); exact year unknown. Owner Alem Gebrehiwot as of 2020 per Wikipedia (citing The Skanner); left out of the copy.
An older guide says no credit cards; likely outdated, left out.
Newest dated evidence it is open: winner, Best Ethiopian, WW readers' poll, Jul 22, 2026 (read from a copy of the page saved earlier this run). A poll win is not a visit.
Fame: WW (readers' poll 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024, 2025, 2026), Eater Portland, KOIN, Portland Mercury and The Skanner. Marked open-secret; a case could be made for local-legend.
Address 2413 NE Martin Luther King Jr Blvd matches Wikipedia.

name: Mi Burrito
why: A long burrito list that reaches cabeza, lamb and tripa carries the signature mark, but cheap burrito shops are common and this is a good version of one. One Willamette Week roundup is all I found, with nothing on the room or its history, so atmosphere and story sit low.
story: Mi Burrito keeps more than 30 burritos on the menu, from asada and pollo to milanesa and chile verde. About a dollar more gets you lamb, cabeza, pork belly or tripa, and you pick whole pinto, black or refried beans. In 2026 it still sold burritos for ten dollars or less.
tagline: Over 30 burritos and three kinds of beans
order: A cabeza or tripa burrito, about a dollar more than the standard ones, with your pick of whole pinto, black or refried beans.
flags: Single source: Willamette Week's ten-dollar burrito roundup, Mar 25, 2026. No own site or second press piece opened.
WW calls it a St. Johns institution, but 819 N Lombard St is near N Interstate, miles east of downtown St. Johns. Area kept as Piedmont from the candidate record; confirm the neighborhood.
A directory lists a Mi Burrito at 2747 N Lombard St, perhaps an older or second shop. WW's 2026 address is 819 N Lombard St.
A directory says it opened in 2015; not used. Founding year and owners unknown.
No description of the room found; the atmosphere mark is a guess.
Closes at 10 pm per WW, so not marked late. Prices as of Mar 2026.
Newest dated evidence it is open: WW, Mar 2026.

name: Barbur World Foods
why: The family story and a deli case cooked in the Ya Hala kitchen carry it. It is a grocery, so the room is aisles and a counter rather than a place to linger, and it is one of three World Foods stores.
story: John and Mirna Attar came to Portland from Lebanon, opened Ya Hala in 1999, and in 2004 took over Barbur Foods, a corner market that had served the neighborhood for decades. The deli case is filled from the Ya Hala kitchen, still overseen by Mirna, and the family runs it with their kids.
tagline: An old corner market stocked by Ya Hala's kitchen
order: Anything in the cold case wearing a Ya Hala sticker, plus pita baked to order in the wood-fired oven.
practical: Smaller sister store at 830 NW Everett St
flags: Locations: three World Foods markets (SW Barbur, NW Everett since 2014, and a small Barbur Foods at PDX airport), per Willamette Week May 2026, plus the family's Ya Hala restaurant. Under our four-location chain line, but worth a look.
Wood-fired pita oven comes from an undated Portland Monthly listing seen only in search results; confirm it still runs.
'Decades' as a corner market is from Portland Monthly 2012; a directory claims 70+ years, which we did not use.
Neighborhood 'Multnomah' is from discovery and not confirmed by a source; it sits at Barbur and Capitol Highway.
A grocery with a deli counter, not a restaurant; no source describes seating.
Closes at 10 pm, so not tagged late.

name: Banning's Restaurant & Pie House
why: A long-running family diner whose scratch pies are the draw; diners are common, but one this old with its own pie case is getting rarer. The story is good but rests mostly on the restaurant's own 2014 blog, and nothing we found describes the room.
story: Brothers Craig and Mark Banning opened in late 1979 in a shuttered restaurant at 69th and Pacific Highway. Mark and his wife Trish, both raised on farms, made it a family place where all three of their kids worked, and for years it ran around the clock. Pies and cakes are made from scratch.
tagline: Scratch pies on Pacific Highway since 1979
order: A slice of pie, baked from scratch daily in more than 20 varieties by the restaurant's own count. At breakfast, the farmer's omelet comes under country gravy.
practical: On Pacific Highway at SW 69th Ave
hours: Mon-Sat 7 am-10 pm, Sun noon-6 pm (Tigard Life, undated; other listings differ)
flags: Open: Banning's Restaurant at 11477 SW Pacific Hwy is in the Valley Times east Washington County inspection roundup published Aug 18, 2026 (read).
History, founders' names, 24-hour era and pie count come from the restaurant's own blog (Dec 2014); current ownership unconfirmed.

Hours conflict: Tigard Life gives Mon-Sat 7 am-10 pm, Sun noon-6 pm; a search summary of another guide gave later weekend hours. No source I opened shows hours past 10 pm, so not tagged late. The 24-hour era appears to be over.
Locations: one (Tigard). Searches found no Beaverton or other branch.

Fame set to open-secret: Tigard Life covered it, a Portland Monthly pie-shop roundup and a Valley Times listing surfaced in searches, and a guide says The Oregonian named its pies among Oregon's best. Only Tigard Life and the own blog are cited.
One listing gives 1177 SW Pacific Hwy; the restaurant's own blog says 11477, matching the candidate.

name: Coredam
why: Marinated raw crab is rare in local restaurants and it is the reason people come, with the banchan and ox bone soup close behind. The story is thin: it opened in 2023 and we found nothing about who runs it.
story: Coredam opened in Central Beaverton in 2023 and is best known for yangnyeom gejang, raw Korean blue crab coated in a thick chile paste and eaten with plastic gloves. A long spread of banchan comes first, and the crowd runs from grandparents to strollers.
tagline: Raw blue crab in chile paste, gloves provided
order: The yangnyeom gejang, then the seolleongtang, a clear ox bone soup in a stone pot that you season with green onion and salt. With a big group, add the budae jeongol, which simmers at the table.
practical: Big group dishes cook at the table on a gas burner
flags: Hours unconfirmed: no source gave them. 'when' (midday, evening) follows discovery's lead and is a guess.
Street address from directory listings only; Portland Monthly names Central Beaverton but no address.
No owner or background found beyond the 2023 opening (Portland Monthly, Apr 2026).
Travel Oregon page seen only in search results (says it drew wide attention at opening for soy-marinated raw crab, rare locally); not opened.
Listings mention long dinner waits and no reservations; not from a citable source, so left out.
Most recent dated coverage: Portland Monthly Beaverton guide, Apr 17, 2026.

name: Sanguiche
why: Italian sandwiches are common, but this one comes with a real family story and a house spice rub. It is brand new, opening in February 2026, and the room is a few tables, so atmosphere stays middling.
story: The Spillettes started with a steak rub Billy worked out at a family dinner, sold it at the Gresham Farmers Market, then added a sandwich booth. In February 2026 the family, with roots in Campania and Sardinia, opened this small downtown shop, which the couple runs with their kids.
tagline: A family spice rub that grew into a sandwich shop
order: The classic Italian is the top seller; the Dimepiece steak sandwich uses the family rub. On Wednesdays, come early for cannoli filled that day, which sell out.
practical: A few tables inside, some outdoor seating
Made to order, so expect a short wait
Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free bread options
flags: Very new: the shop had its grand opening Feb 1, 2026, after a farmers market booth in 2025.
Single source: The Outlook feature (Mar 10, 2026). Own site sanguicheshop.com is named there but did not turn up in search and was not opened.
Hours from March 2026; the owners said they were considering evening hours, so check.
Open status rests on the March 2026 article; delivery listings suggest it is still running, but those are not sources.

name: Las Brasas
why: Costa Rican cooking is hard to find around here, and the owner has been on chicken duty since 1982, so uniqueness and story hold up. The room is a plain converted laundromat, it only opened in February 2026, and one local paper is all the press so far.
story: Jorge Zuniga started cooking chicken in 1982 at another restaurant named Las Brasas. He and his wife Zoraida opened Casa de Pollo down the block in 2005, later moved it to Lake Oswego, then took two years off. This Costa Rican rotisserie is the comeback, in a rebuilt former laundromat.
tagline: Costa Rican rotisserie in a former laundromat
order: The marinated rotisserie chicken, which you can watch turning from the counter, as a casado plate with rice and beans. Ask for Zoraida's chimichurri.
practical: At the corner of Division and Main
Ceviche on Fridays and Saturdays only
Whole roast chicken family meal available
hours: Mon-Sat 10 am-8 pm, Sun 11 am-5 pm (Gresham Outlook, Feb 2026)
flags: Single source: everything comes from the Gresham Outlook opening feature (Feb 16, 2026). No other press, own site or neighborhood blog found; Instagram is @lasbrasasgresham per that article (not checked).
Most recent dated evidence is that Feb 2026 article. The discovery note cites a Sep 2026 county inspection, but I could not find it within budget.
Open less than a year (opened Feb 5, 2026).
Hours are from the Feb 2026 article and not rechecked.
The article does not say where the 1982 Las Brasas was (probably Costa Rica); the story avoids saying.

name: Murata
why: Tatami rooms and a family owner since 1988 make it rarer than the average downtown Japanese spot, and the weekday lunch set keeps getting recommended. We found little story beyond the ownership date, and it is widely covered, so nobody would call it a secret.
story: This Japanese restaurant in the 200 Market office building has been owned by one family since 1988, and it holds a sushi bar and three tatami rooms. Guidebooks have long noted its crowd of locals and Japanese businesspeople, and Portland critics still put it on their best-of lists.
tagline: Three tatami rooms in a downtown office building
order: The weekday teishoku lunch: pick a protein, anything from sashimi to fried chicken, and it comes with rice, pickles and cucumber salad. Call a few days ahead if you want a tatami room. At dinner, critics say skip the set menus for nigiri a la carte.
practical: Parking validation in the 200 Market building garage
hours: Weekday lunch from 11:30 am, last call 1:30 pm; dinner Mon-Sat from about 5 or 5:30 pm to 8:30 or 9 pm; closed Sun (own site for lunch and Sunday; dinner times from Time Out and Portland Monthly listings, which disagree)
flags: Status unclear: no dated evidence it is open since Nov 2025. Confirm before approving.

Still-open check is soft: I found no dated evidence from after Nov 2025. The own site is live with lunch specials and phone reservations (undated), Wikipedia (read Oct 2026) shows no closure, and its newest cited coverage is Time Out's 2025 best-restaurants list. A Time Out list titled 2026 came up in search but I could not confirm Murata is on it. Worth a call before approving.

Fit check: Time Out puts dinner at about $40 or more a head, and The Oregonian (2024, via Wikipedia) says weekend dinner tables are hard to get. Drafted as a lunch spot; you may judge it too reservation-driven for the guide.
Dinner hours differ between Time Out (5-8:30 pm) and Portland Monthly (5:30-9 pm) listings; the own site, seen only as a search snippet, confirms lunch last call 1:30 pm and closed Sundays.
Teishoku details and garage validation come from an undated Portland Monthly lunch guide, seen as a search snippet.
'Since 1988' is when the current family took ownership (Wikipedia citing Portland Monthly); the opening year was not found.
Heavily covered (Portland Monthly top 50 in 2024, The Oregonian, Eater Portland, Time Out, The Infatuation, Fodor's); local-legend would also be defensible.

name: Republic Cafe and Ming Lounge
why: A century in one family's hands in what is left of Old Town Chinatown, so uniqueness and story run high. Signature is low because no source we can use names a dish to get, and current hours are unconfirmed.
story: The Mui family opened this Old Town Chinatown dining room in 1922, going by the date printed on its menus, and still runs it. The restaurant counts Louis Armstrong and Shaquille O'Neal among past guests. In 2026 it got a plum-blossom mural, the flowers picked as a sign of Chinatown's staying power.
tagline: One family's Chinatown dining room since 1922
order: Dinner in the old dining room, then a drink in the Ming Lounge, the bar that shares its name.
practical: Plum-blossom mural on the building since 2026
flags: Founding year: 1922 is the family's date, confirmed in Willamette Week (May 15, 2026). WW's 2023 piece says the owners go by the date printed on the menus, and at least one other account gives 1927 (others say about 1930). The story says 'going by the date printed on its menus' to stay honest.

Hours unconfirmed. Portland Monthly's listing shows 8 am to midnight daily, which looks stale. Hoodline and a similar rewritten page (Feb 2026, not citable) say lunch stopped after the pandemic and it is dinner only; 'when' is set to evening on that basis and `late` is left off. Call to confirm.
'One of the last two Chinese restaurants in Old Town Chinatown' rests only on Hoodline and AI-rewritten pages, so it is left out of the copy.
No sourced signature dish; 'order' names the dining room and the Ming Lounge only.
Famous guests are as listed by the restaurant and the Portland Street Art Alliance, reported by WW.
Most recent dated evidence: WW mural story, May 15, 2026.

name: The Sultan Cafe
why: A good, cheap, owner-run Middle Eastern counter that press keeps returning to for value, which is a common thing done well. The room is plain and the history we found is one early Willamette Week visit.
story: Owner Maher Makboul runs this Slabtown Middle Eastern grill, featured in past Willamette Week cheap eats guides, and Axios named it one of the city's underrated spots in 2024. An early WW write-up found the owner back then had quit managing a bar and bid on the building the day he saw it.
tagline: Owner-run Middle Eastern grill in Slabtown
order: The Jerusalem-style manakeesh, or the falafel bowl with salad. Shawarma if you want meat.
hours: Mon-Fri 8:30 am-5 pm, Sat 11 am-3 pm, closed Sun (own site, seen as a search snippet)
flags: Open: Willamette Week quotes Maher Makboul as owner on June 26, 2026.

Hours conflict: the own site shows weekdays 8:30 am-5 pm and Sat 11 am-3 pm, while a Portland Mercury listing shows 7 am-6 pm weekdays and to 1 am Fri-Sat. I used the own site, so 'when' is morning and midday, not evening as discovery had it. Please confirm.

The early WW piece ('Old Is New') is undated (old URL format) and was seen only as a search snippet. It names a Michael Makboul; the 2026 owner is Maher Makboul. Could be the same person or a relative, so the story says 'the owner back then' without a name.
Dishes come from the Axios list (May 2024); the current menu was not checked.
Discovery's address matches the own site (1500 NW 18th Ave, Suite 101); the Mercury listing says NW 18th St, likely a typo.

name: Goose Hollow Inn
why: A tavern opened by a future mayor that gave the neighborhood back its name, still in his family, with a Reuben that is its whole reputation. It is on every list, and at heart it is a tavern with one famous sandwich, which keeps uniqueness out of the 90s.
story: Bud Clark bought Ann's Tavern at SW 19th and Jefferson in 1967 after the city razed his old bar, and named it to revive a lost neighborhood name. He went on to be mayor while his wife Sigrid ran the place. The Clark family still owns it, and the Reuben is the point.
tagline: A future mayor's tavern, family-run since 1967
order: The Reuben: corned beef and Reuben sauce, toasted on rye. Pair it with a pint and take it out to the deck under the birch trees.
practical: No video poker, just one TV
hours: Daily from 11 am, to midnight most nights and 1 am Fridays (Portland Monthly listing, undated)
flags: Status unclear: no dated evidence it is open since Nov 2025. Confirm before approving.

No dated sign of life since Nov 2025 found within budget. The own site speaks in the present tense (still going strong, daughter Rachel manages) but is undated; the March 2026 travel guide in the discovery note was not seen.
Hours and `late` rest on an undated Portland Monthly listing (WW's 2015 bar guide had the same hours). Directory listings show 10 to 11 pm closings, so confirm before keeping `late`.
The discovery lead's 'Reuben goes through a pizza oven' was not confirmed by anything I could read, so it is left out.
The own site gives Bud Clark's mayoral term as both 1985-1992 and 1985-1993; the story avoids the years.
Story facts are mostly from the tavern's own site, backed on the naming and Reuben by WW and Wikipedia.

name: Devil's Dill
why: Being the city's late-night deli is a real niche in an early-closing town, and readers still vote for it. We found almost nothing about the room or a signature sandwich, and the story is mostly the hours.
story: Devil's Dill has made sandwiches on Hawthorne since 2013, and its name rests on serving them late: as of 2025 it was the city's only late-night deli. A second shop opened on NE Killingsworth in 2025, and Willamette Week readers ranked it second for late-night eats in 2026.
order: A hot sandwich after 10 pm, which is the whole reason people know it. Check the Hawthorne hours before you go, since they have moved around over the years.
hours: Sun-Tue until 11 pm, Wed-Sat until 1 am; opening time not confirmed (Wikipedia, as of 2025; own site lists no hours)
flags: Status unclear: the Hawthorne shop may be closed after a September 2026 fire in its building (Wikipedia, seen in search results). Confirm before approving.

Wikipedia (seen in search results) says a fire damaged the building housing the Hawthorne shop in September 2026. I could not confirm whether the shop is open now. The own site still offers online ordering from Hawthorne. Confirm before publishing.

Late hours (to 1 am Wed-Sat, 11 pm other nights) come from Wikipedia as of 2025, seen in search results only; the own site lists no hours. Older listings show 3 am closing (WW 2017). Re-check, especially after the fire.
Opening time unconfirmed from a usable source, so midday is left off `when`; directory listings show an 11 am opening.
No specific sandwich sourced; `order` rests on the late-night reputation.
Two locations, under the chain line: Hawthorne and NE Killingsworth (own site gives 1620 NE Killingsworth; Bridgetown Bites gave 5470 NE 16th Ave for the same shop).
Willamette Week 2026 readers' poll also lists it as a finalist for Best Sandwich Shop (July 22, 2026).

name: Cricket Cafe
why: A steady Belmont breakfast room with a genuine comeback story and a menu that works for mixed diets. Nothing here is one of a kind, and no usable source names a standout dish.
story: Cricket Cafe has been cooking breakfast on Belmont since 1999. It closed without warning in June 2017, then reopened under new owners who kept the menu mostly as it was and added more vegan and gluten-free plates.
order: Breakfast for a table with mixed diets, since the menu carries vegan and gluten-free versions alongside the usual plates. Come early on weekdays: the kitchen stops at 1 pm.
hours: Mon-Fri 8 am-1 pm, Sat-Sun 8 am-2 pm (own site)
flags: Status unclear: no dated evidence it is open since Nov 2025. Confirm before approving.

No dated evidence that it is open since Nov 2025. The own site lists current hours and takeout but carries no date. Discovery cited Travel Portland's Belmont guide (said to be revised in 2026), which this environment can't open. Confirm it's open before publishing.

June 2017 closing, reopening under new owners and the added vegan and gluten-free dishes come from Wikipedia, Willamette Week (Oct 2017) and the Portland Mercury (Jan 2018) as seen in search results; I did not open those pages.
Most recent dated press found is from 2018.
No specific dish sourced. Reviews mention a vegan skillet, but only on sites we can't cite.
Older listings give different hours (daily to 2:30 pm in 2018); own site hours used.

name: Space Room Lounge
why: A 1959 bar that still commits to its outer-space theme is a room you remember, and it shows up on every dive list. The food and drink are serviceable rather than the reason to go, and no source names a signature.
story: The Space Room has poured drinks on Hawthorne since 1959 under an outer-space theme it never outgrew. In 2014 it joined up with Genie's, which is why breakfast runs all day beside the bar. Willamette Week readers voted it the city's best dive bar in 2017.
tagline: Outer-space dive bar on Hawthorne since 1959
order: Breakfast at the bar at whatever hour you turn up, since the kitchen serves it all day. Come before 3 pm if you're bringing kids.
hours: Mon-Fri 11 am-1 am, Sat-Sun 10 am-1 am (own site)
flags: Most recent dated press is Portland Monthly's dive bar guide, Nov 21, 2025, seen in search results only; the own site lists current hours but is undated.
Founding year (1959), the 2014 merger with Genie's and the 2017 readers' poll come from Wikipedia, seen in search results only.
An older Portland Monthly listing shows a 2:30 am close; the own site now says 1 am. Own site used.
No standout dish or drink sourced from a usable source; `order` rests on the all-day breakfast from the own site.
Fame set to local-legend: open since 1959 and a regular in Portland Monthly and Willamette Week dive bar coverage. Reviewer may prefer open-secret.

name: Lauretta Jean's
why: The pie is the point, and Portland Monthly calls it unrivaled in town. The room and the market-stall-to-storefront story are pleasant but ordinary, and Division is a busy, well-covered strip.
story: Kate McMillen started Lauretta Jean's as a Portland Farmers Market stall, ran a small takeout counter downtown, then moved into the old Pix Pâtisserie space on Division in 2012. Division is the only shop it lists today. The tart cherry pie is billed as a Grandma Jean original.
tagline: Farmers market pies, on Division since 2012
order: A slice of the tart cherry, a Grandma Jean recipe under a lattice top. Slices are sold every day but Tuesday, and whole pies can be ordered by phone the day before.
practical: Call a day ahead for whole pies
hours: Mon, Wed, Thu 11 am-9 pm; Fri-Sat 9 am-10 pm; Sun 9 am-9 pm; closed Tue (own site, Oct 2026)
flags: Location count: the own site lists one shop, 3402 SE Division (address confirmed). Wikipedia still describes two locations; the downtown SW Pine Street shop appears closed, but I found no dated report of the closing.
Farmers market start and the downtown takeout shop come from Wikipedia, seen in search results only.
Fri-Sat close at 10 pm, not past it, so `late` is left off.
Price ($7 a slice) from the own site, Oct 2026.
Most recent dated coverage: Portland Monthly's Clinton and Division guide, Feb 27, 2026. Own site is current (Thanksgiving orders open Nov 2).
Well known on a tourist-heavy strip; reviewer may judge it too familiar for the guide.

name: Scottie's Pizza Parlor
why: The slice is why you come, and Portland Monthly says many rank it the city's best. The Division shop is barely a room, one booth and two outdoor tables, and pizza is a crowded field here.
story: Brooklyn-born Scott Rivera opened Scottie's on Division in July 2015, after stints at Ava Gene's and Baby Doll Pizza. Naturally leavened dough from Northwest wheat goes into a very hot electric deck oven and comes out New York style, sold by the slice or as an 18-inch pie. A second shop runs on NW 21st.
order: A slice or two at the counter, or the 16-inch square grandma pie if there are a few of you. Seating is one booth and two uncovered picnic tables, so on a wet day take it home.
practical: One booth inside, two uncovered tables out front
flags: Two locations, under the chain line: 2128 SE Division and 685 NW 21st Ave (own site).
Owner's background (Brooklyn-born, earlier work at Ava Gene's and Baby Doll Pizza) and the July 2015 opening come from Wikipedia, seen in search results only.
Most recent dated coverage: Portland Monthly's Clinton and Division guide, Feb 27, 2026. Own site is undated.
No named specialty pie sourced from press; `order` uses the slice and the grandma pie from the own site.
